lesson.title: The Americas Before 1492: A World Already Full of Nations
lesson.summary: This section introduces the deep human history of the Americas before European contact, showing that the continents were home to millions of people living in sophisticated, varied societies for thousands of years before 1492.
lesson.body:
For most of human history, the Americas developed almost entirely apart from Europe, Africa, and Asia. The first people to arrive came from northeastern Asia, most likely crossing into Alaska during the last Ice Age, when lower sea levels exposed a land bridge across the Bering Strait known as Beringia. Exactly when this happened is still debated among archaeologists. Some evidence points to human presence as early as twenty thousand years ago, while more conservative estimates place the first substantial migrations closer to thirteen thousand years ago. What is certain is that over many centuries, small groups of hunter gatherers spread south and east, eventually reaching the southern tip of South America and populating two entire continents.

The term pre-Columbian simply means before the voyages of Christopher Columbus in 1492. It does not mean simple or unchanging. By the time European ships appeared off American shores, the Western Hemisphere held an enormous range of societies, from small mobile bands who hunted, fished, and gathered wild plants, to dense cities governed by kings, priests, and bureaucracies. Hundreds of distinct languages were spoken, often as different from one another as English is from Mandarin. Some peoples built empires that stretched across mountain ranges and coastlines. Others lived in small, self governing communities that had no need for centralized rule at all. There was no single Native American way of life, any more than there was a single European way of life.

One development changed nearly everything: agriculture. In the highlands of southern Mexico, people began domesticating a wild grass called teosinte into what we now know as maize, or corn, thousands of years before Columbus was born. Over time, farmers across Mesoamerica learned to grow maize alongside beans and squash, a combination so effective that later peoples called it the Three Sisters. Corn alone is a poor source of certain nutrients, but beans and squash fill the gaps, and beans are nitrogen fixing plants that replenish soil that corn depletes. This package of crops spread both south into the Andes and north into what is now the United States, allowing populations to grow, settle in one place, and build permanent towns and cities.

The results of that agricultural revolution were dramatic. In central Mexico, cities arose that were, by the time of European contact, among the largest urban centers anywhere in the world, rivaling or exceeding the populations of London or Paris. Farther north, along the Mississippi River and its tributaries, farming communities raised massive earthen mounds as centers of religious and political life. Trade networks connected peoples across thousands of miles, moving copper from the Great Lakes, seashells from the Gulf Coast, and obsidian from volcanic highlands into the hands of people who had never traveled more than a few days from home.

This section sets the stage for everything that follows. The chapters ahead will look closely at particular regions and peoples: the many distinct cultures of North America, the imperial power of the Aztec state in central Mexico, and the mound building societies of the Mississippi Valley. Keep in mind as you read that these were not static, frozen worlds waiting for Europeans to discover them. They were dynamic societies with their own histories of growth, conflict, migration, and change, and that history did not stop in 1492. It continued, transformed by contact with a new and unfamiliar set of peoples arriving from across the Atlantic.
